# Results — Study 241 (Buy-the-Dip) on real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Systematic dip-buying
on SPY: wait for a drawdown of X% from the running all-time high, buy at the next
open, exit when a new ATH close is made. Grid of thresholds (2%, 5%, 10%, 15%, 20%)
vs always-invested buy-and-hold and vs DCA. Cash earns 0% while waiting (and 4% in
a sensitivity test). One-way cost = 1 bp. As-of **2026-06-16**; match the
fingerprint to confirm you hold the same tape.*

## Data stamp

| Ticker | Window | Days | Fingerprint |
|---|---|--:|---|
| SPY | 1993-01-29 → 2026-06-16 | 8,402 | `06520b76c02a` |

## Buy-and-hold benchmark

| Metric | Value |
|---|--:|
| CAGR | **+10.86%/yr** |
| Sharpe (annualised) | **0.648** |
| Max drawdown | −55.2% |
| Period | 33.4 years |

## Dip-buying vs buy-and-hold — the main result

All thresholds, zero cash rate (pure cash drag):

| Threshold | Buys | Frac. in market | DB CAGR | BH CAGR | CAGR vs BH | HAC *t* (daily excess) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2% | 92 | 72.3% | +9.06% | +10.86% | **−1.80%** | −1.88 |
| 5% | 36 | 58.1% | +7.58% | +10.86% | **−3.27%** | **−2.53** |
| 10% | 12 | 47.1% | +4.37% | +10.86% | **−6.49%** | **−4.05** |
| 15% | 7 | 39.6% | +4.12% | +10.86% | **−6.74%** | **−3.80** |
| 20% | 4 | 34.9% | +3.20% | +10.86% | **−7.66%** | **−4.03** |

**Every threshold underperforms buy-and-hold.** The gap widens as the threshold
increases because larger dips are rarer — the investor sits in non-performing cash
for longer. The HAC *t*-stats on the daily excess returns are all negative; four of
five exceed |*t*| = 2 (two-sided), confirming the underperformance is statistically
real and not sampling noise.

## DCA comparison

Dollar-cost averaging (equal monthly installments) also underperforms buy-and-hold:

| Strategy | CAGR | vs BH |
|---|--:|--:|
| Buy-and-hold | +10.86% | — |
| DCA (monthly) | +6.74% | **−4.11%** |
| Dip-buy 5% | +7.58% | −3.27% |
| Dip-buy 10% | +4.37% | −6.49% |

DCA underperforms because it delays full deployment of capital (cash drag), just
like dip-buying. Both are dominated by immediate full investment.

## Sensitivity: cash earning a 4% annual rate

Even with cash earning ~4% p.a. (a T-bill proxy), every dip-buying threshold still
underperforms buy-and-hold:

| Threshold | DB CAGR (4% cash) | BH CAGR | CAGR vs BH |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 5% | +9.37% | +10.86% | **−1.49%** |
| 10% | +6.56% | +10.86% | **−4.30%** |
| 20% | +5.87% | +10.86% | **−4.99%** |

The risk-free rate closes the gap at tight thresholds (2%, 5%) but never closes it
completely, and deeper thresholds still lose badly.

## Why it fails — the cash-drag mechanism

The dip-buying investor is out of the market a significant fraction of the time
(28–65%, depending on threshold). During secular bull markets, that time out is
spent watching the market rise without them. Even if dips do tend to recover (which
they do — the 10% dip buyer's in-market CAGR is reasonable), the compounded effect
of missing the up-days in cash more than offsets any cheapness in entry prices.

The key insight: in a market with positive drift (~10.9%/yr for SPY), **time in
the market matters more than timing the market**. The dip-buyer reduces their time
in the market in exchange for a modest improvement in average entry price — a trade
that is structurally negative in expectation.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** Every threshold underperforms buy-and-hold, with HAC
  *t* of daily excess returns ranging from −1.88 (2% threshold) to −4.05 (10%
  threshold). The effect is statistically the opposite of the claimed edge.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** The strategy is implementable but there is no edge to
  trade; the cash drag systematically destroys returns relative to passive buy-and-hold.
  Even generous cash returns (4% p.a.) do not rescue the rule.
- **Myth check — BUSTED.** "Buy the dip" beats staying invested: this is false on
  SPY across 33 years and all reasonable threshold definitions.
